title: Corporate culture

match.reason: The bank point defines corporate culture and links it to morale and turnover, but it does not teach the new point's distinction between official stated values and real staff behaviour, or how managers shape culture through rewards, symbols and example, so adding those would be a new idea rather than a small change.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, wording: The right option is the only hedged one ('tend to'), echoing the card's wording. The other three are flat claims, so a student could pick it from the qualifier alone.

rejected.title: Corporate culture
card: Official culture
the values a business states, such as in a mission statement or on its website.
Real culture
how staff actually behave day to day. It may match the official culture or differ from it.
Managers can shape culture through rewards, such as praise or bonuses for the behaviour they want.
They can also use symbols, such as logos, uniforms or awards, and their own example. Staff watch what managers do, and tend to follow actions over words.
rejected.remember: Culture is both what a business says and what staff do. Managers can shape it through rewards, symbols and example.

a.q: A firm says it values teamwork, but staff mostly work alone and rarely help each other. What does this show?
opts: Its real culture differs from its official culture
Its official culture is its real culture
Its managers have used rewards well
Its staff follow its stated values closely
a.why: The stated value is teamwork, but behaviour shows otherwise, so real culture differs from official culture. The official culture is only what is stated, not what happens.
a.clue: Compare what the firm says with what staff do.

b.q: Priya's bakery in Geelong says 'customers first' on its website, and staff wear badges saying so. Priya often leaves complaints unanswered to finish paperwork. What is most likely?
opts: Staff tend to copy her and put complaints aside
Staff follow the website, as it states the values
The badges lead staff to put customers first
Official culture changes to match her behaviour
b.why: Staff watch what managers do and tend to follow actions over words, so Priya's example is likely to shape the real culture. The website and badges are tempting, but they state values that her own behaviour contradicts. Official culture is the stated values, so her actions change the real culture, not the official one.
b.clue: Think about whose behaviour staff look to.

b.q: Sam, a café owner in Ballarat, wants staff to value punctuality. What is the strongest step from the card to shape this?
opts: Arrive on time himself and reward punctual staff
Print punctuality in the menu and do nothing else
Say it once and expect staff to guess the rest
Reward staff only for sales, not for their behaviour
b.why: Staff watch what managers do, and rewards encourage the behaviour wanted, so Sam's own example plus rewards shapes culture. Only stating the value risks leaving real culture different.

a.best: Its real culture differs from its official culture

b.best: Arrive on time himself and reward punctual staff

problems.detail: The distractors are obviously poor choices ('expect staff to guess the rest', 'do nothing else', reward only for sales), so a Year 12 student can pick the answer without knowing the idea. The question tests little.
The right option stands out. It is the only one that names constructive actions, and it matches the clue 'example and rewards' word for word. The others are framed as plainly negative.
'Culture is shown by what staff do' describes only real culture. It leaves out official culture, the stated values the card defines as part of culture, so it narrows what the card teaches.

check.summary: The card and Question a are accurate. Question b is too easy because its distractors are absurd and the right option echoes the clue. The remember line describes only real culture and omits official culture.
